fatal_errors: The base Ti–Ni alloy composition is unspecified, so the phase stability, Mo solubility, aging response, and applicability of the proposed treatment cannot be assessed.

The cited evidence concerns compositionally different Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni and Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ni alloys and does not establish that 2–3 at.% Mo plus aging at 700 °C for 5 hours will generate strengthening precipitates in the target Ti–Ni alloy.
The intervention combines Mo addition and aging without Mo-only, aging-only, and untreated controls, preventing attribution of any improvement to either component.
The proposed sigma-versus-L12 structural mediator is underdetermined, and the claimed 20–30% strength increase is unsupported by the cited evidence.
explanation: The hypothesis is testable and broadly aligned with improving elevated-temperature performance in a Ti–Ni-containing HEA, but it does not reconstruct the target intervention. The target used laser-assisted machining of a specific DED-fabricated Ti33Nb28Cr11V11Ni17 alloy, exploiting strong thermal softening near or above 800 °C to reduce cutting force, roughness, and machining-induced work hardening. The generated hypothesis instead proposes alloying and precipitation aging at 700 °C, with an entirely different mechanism and outcome. Its evidence supports the generic possibility of Mo-associated sigma strengthening or nanoscale precipitation in other HEAs, but extrapolation to an unspecified Ti–Ni alloy, the selected aging schedule, the proposed phase identity, and the numerical strength gain is weak. A factorial experiment with untreated, aging-only, Mo-only, and Mo-plus-aging groups, together with phase-equilibrium characterization and replicated high-temperature tests, would make the alternative substantially more discriminating.
